draft.title: Parties to a civil dispute
card: Plaintiff
the person or group who brings the civil claim. They say they have been wronged and ask the court for a remedy.
Defendant
the person or group who answers the claim. They may be an individual, a business or a government body.
A civil dispute is between these two parties. The plaintiff starts it, and the defendant responds to it.
Class action
a claim brought by one person on behalf of a group of at least seven people who have been wronged in a similar way. The group members share the same type of complaint against the same defendant.
draft.remember: The plaintiff sues and the defendant answers. A class action lets one person act for a group.

a.q: Which description fits the defendant in a civil dispute?
opts: The party who responds to the claim made against them
The party who starts the claim and asks for a remedy
The party who decides which side wins the dispute
The party who is always a business or a company
a.why: The defendant is the party who answers the claim. The plaintiff is the one who starts it. A defendant can be an individual, a business or a government body, so it is not always a company.
a.clue: Think about who is being claimed against.

b.q: Hundreds of customers of a Geelong gym were overcharged in the same way. Ana brings one claim for all of them against the gym. Who is the plaintiff, and what is the claim called?
opts: Ana, in a class action against the gym
The gym, in a class action against Ana
Ana, in a claim where each customer is a defendant
The customers, with the gym as the plaintiff
b.why: Ana starts the claim, so she is the plaintiff. She acts for a group with a similar complaint against the same defendant, so it is a class action. The gym answers the claim, so it is the defendant. The other group members are not defendants.
b.clue: Who starts the claim, and who answers it?

a.best: The party who responds to the claim made against them

b.best: Ana, in a class action against the gym

problems.detail: The distractor 'The party who is always a business or a company' uses 'always' where the card says a defendant 'may be' an individual, business or government body. The absolute word marks it as wrong without testing the idea.

check.summary: The card is accurate: in Victoria a group proceeding needs seven or more people, and both questions have one clear right answer. The only minor issue is that one distractor in question a uses 'always', which makes it easy to rule out.
